lesson.title: Three Stops for a Memory: The Multi-Store Model
lesson.summary: The multi-store memory model proposes that information passes through three distinct memory systems, sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory, each with its own capacity and duration, on its way to being permanently retained.
lesson.body:
The multi-store memory model, developed by Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin in 1968, proposes that memory is not one single system but a sequence of three distinct stores that information passes through on its way to being permanently retained. An incoming stimulus first enters sensory memory, an extremely brief holding stage. If attention is paid to it, the information moves into short-term memory, a limited-capacity, limited-duration workspace. If that information is then rehearsed or meaningfully processed, it can move into long-term memory, a store with a much greater capacity and duration. Each of the three stores differs in how much information it can hold and for how long, and information that is not passed along at each transition point tends to be lost rather than retained.

The model is a good illustration of psychology functioning as a science, since it was built to generate testable predictions that could be checked against actual behavior. One of the clearest pieces of supporting evidence is the serial position effect, the finding that when people try to recall a list of items, they tend to remember the first few items well, known as the primacy effect, and the last few items well, known as the recency effect, while items in the middle are recalled worst. The multi-store model explains this directly: early items had time to be rehearsed into long-term memory, while the most recent items are still sitting in short-term memory at recall, and only the middle items have been pushed out of both without being adequately transferred.

The very first stage of the model depends on a concept from the study of sensation and perception: the absolute threshold, the minimum intensity a stimulus needs to be detected at all. A stimulus has to cross this threshold before it can register in sensory memory, since a signal too faint to be sensed cannot begin the memory process. This links the model directly to the basic question of what counts as a detectable stimulus, showing that memory does not start from raw physical energy in the environment but from whatever portion of that energy the senses are capable of registering.

Because the model treats sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory as genuinely separate systems, each deserves closer examination: its capacity, how long information lasts within it, and what causes information to be lost if not transferred onward. The outline here, information flowing from a fleeting sensory trace, through a small working space, into a lasting store, is the map that later, more detailed exploration of each store follows.

Since 1968, researchers have refined and complicated this original picture considerably. Short-term memory, for instance, is now often understood less as one unified box and more as a multi-component working memory system, with separate storage for verbal and visual-spatial information alongside a controlling attentional system. There is also evidence that the stores interact more flexibly than a strict one-way pipeline suggests, with some information reaching long-term memory without extensive rehearsal, and long-term knowledge shaping how information is processed in short-term memory in the first place. Even so, the basic three-store architecture remains a valuable foundational framework, because it correctly captures the broad separation in capacity and duration between fleeting sensory impressions, momentarily held information, and lasting memories, even where the real underlying system turns out to be more interactive than the original model assumed.
